source.title: Crown, Frame, Reverse: Layer-Wise Scaling Variants for LLM Pre-Training

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, with minor extraction and formatting errors.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether architectural changes at a roughly fixed parameter budget affect validation loss, using layer-wise parameter allocation variants rather than scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The study compares layer-wise architectural variants at about 180M parameters and 5B training tokens. It does not sweep model size, token count, or compute, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It reports that benchmark evaluation was abandoned; cited results from other studies are not its own results.
record.test_reason: The study trains isotropic and layer-wise-scaled models at a roughly fixed 180M-parameter budget on 5B tokens and compares held-out validation loss. That bears directly on V4, whether shape changes loss only slightly at fixed parameter count. It fits no laws and sweeps no scale, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that all LWS variants improve validation perplexity (up to ~5%) over an equal-parameter isotropic baseline, and that the exact profile matters little: gains are incremental. They find LWS alone does not reproduce OpenELM's claimed 2x data efficiency. They also find that LWS helps only at 18 layers, not 12, and they caution about a single small scale, single runs and perplexity-only evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting loss laws across model, token, or compute scales, the study trains fixed-budget layer-wise architecture variants and compares validation loss and perplexity.
record.method_sensitivity: The 12-layer vanilla comparison is described as insignificant, while the 18-layer comparison is meaningful; the tested 18-layer LWS profiles perform similarly. The LWS variants were single runs, unlike the five baseline 18L runs.
record.problems: The experiments cover one small model scale and 5B tokens. LWS variants were run once, while the 18-layer baseline was run five times; the table reports a baseline standard deviation of 0.0595 without identifying the metric. The authors also note that the validation data may share the training distribution and that benchmark and generated-text evaluation were not feasible at this scale.
record.rows_left_out: Training cross-entropy is shown in Figures 6–7 but is not held-out validation loss, so it is not included as a row for V4. Tokens-per-second results are not measurements of the claim versions. No relevant validation-loss rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Only one model scale (~180M) and one token budget (5B) are tested. Only two depths (12, 18) and four layer-wise profiles are compared. No sweep of aspect ratio, heads or FFN ratio over a wide range, and no other model sizes.
Not tested: there is no sweep of parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: no small-run fits are extrapolated to larger runs.
Not tested: there is no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
Not tested: only text pretraining is studied.
Not tested: benchmark evaluation was abandoned.
Not tested: no fitting choices or exponents are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The evidence is weak: LWS variants are single runs; the 0.0595 SD has no named metric (likely perplexity); and validation data comes from the same distribution as training (unusually low perplexity ~5). The 12L vs 18L isotropic comparison confounds depth with FFN/attention ratio changes. Training loss appears only in figures, and tokens-per-second results do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of parameters, tokens, or compute to test power-law loss behavior.
No small-run fits or predictions evaluated on larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or optimization of parameter and token counts.
Tests several layer-wise allocations and 12- versus 18-layer settings at one small model scale; does not test a wide range of architecture details or model sizes.
Only text pretraining is studied; no other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance results; the paper says benchmark evaluation was infeasible at this scale.
Does not compare scaling-law fitting choices or estimate scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: BASELINE 12L
rows.check: Control row; its state is correctly cannot_determine. It also serves as the reference for R3's depth/width comparison.

rows.subject: VANILLA LWS 12L
rows.note: The paper describes the 12-layer difference as insignificant.

rows.subject: BASELINE 18L
rows.note: Isotropic reference for the 18-layer variants. The table note reports a standard deviation of 0.0595 for the baseline's last step but does not specify the metric.
rows.check: R3 is a V4 result in its own right, not only a control. Going from 12 to 18 layers with narrower FFN and attention, at similar parameters, raises validation loss from 1.6018 to 1.6864 (~5%; perplexity 4.962 to 5.400). Its baseline should be BASELINE 12L (1.6018). The table note gives an SD of 0.0595 for this baseline's last step without naming the metric; the value may be a mean of five runs, which the text does not say.

rows.subject: VANILLA LWS 18L
rows.note: The paper describes this as a meaningful improvement; its reported validation perplexity is about 6% better than the 18-layer baseline.
rows.check: Loss falls 0.058 vs the 18L baseline (~3.5%). The authors call this meaningful (6% better perplexity). The shape change has a small but significant effect, so partial is right.

rows.subject: FRAMED LWS
rows.note: The paper says this variant had a higher final perplexity than the other LWS variants, but does not conclude it was worse because its curve had a late bump.
rows.check: Loss falls 0.037 vs the 18L baseline (~2%). The authors note a late perplexity bump, so the final value may understate this variant.

rows.subject: REVERSE LWS
rows.note: The paper groups the 18-layer variants as performing almost the same and better than the isotropic baseline.

rows.subject: CROWN LWS
rows.note: The paper groups the 18-layer variants as performing almost the same and better than the isotropic baseline.

relationships.condition: Choice among layer-wise profiles at 18 layers, and vanilla LWS vs isotropic at 12 layers, ~180M params, 5B tokens
relationships.reason: The four 18L LWS profiles span only 1.6206–1.6490 loss (R4–R7), and the authors say the exact profile matters little. The 12L LWS vs baseline gap (1.6062 vs 1.6018, R2 vs R1) is called insignificant.
relationships.display_finding: Four 18-layer profiles had losses of 1.6206–1.6490, while the 12-layer scaled and isotropic models differed insignificantly at 1.6062 versus 1.6018.

source_check.reason: R4–R7 span losses 1.6206–1.6490, and the authors describe profile choice as having little effect. R1–R2 differ insignificantly at 12 layers.

relationships.condition: Isotropic vs layer-wise allocation, and 12- vs 18-layer depth/width trade, at fixed ~180M params
relationships.reason: Redistributing width across layers lowers loss by 2–4% vs the 18L isotropic baseline, which the authors call significant (R3–R7). The 12→18-layer trade raises loss ~5% (R1 vs R3). Shape effects are thus small but not negligible at this scale; LWS runs are single-seed.
relationships.display_finding: Redistributing width reduced loss by 2–4% relative to the 18-layer isotropic baseline, while changing from 12 to 18 layers raised loss by about 5%; layerwise allocation experiments used single seeds.

source_check.condition: Isotropic vs layer-wise allocation, and 12- vs 18-layer depth/width trade, at fixed ~180M params
source_check.reason: R3–R7 show modest but author-described significant improvements from heterogeneous allocation; R1 versus R3 also shows a depth/width preference. These qualify how little shape matters without establishing a reversal of V4.
